title: Template Injection
summary: Template injection abuses the document properties that tell an office application where to fetch shared resources. Modern Office files are ZIP containers of XML parts, and one part may hold a template reference, a pointer to a formatted blueprint that the application retrieves when the document is opened. Because that pointer is just data inside the package, an adversary can repoint it at a server they control, so the payload is not stored in the document at all and only arrives at open time. Static inspection then finds a file with no macro, no script and no embedded executable, which defeats reviewers and signature checks that expect a self-contained threat. The same idea exists in the older rich text format, where the template control word names a destination resource that is retrieved when the file loads, and the bytes of that control word can be altered so simple pattern matching misses it. A related objective is credential theft rather than code execution: a remote reference to a resource on an attacker-controlled server makes the victim's client authenticate, and the resulting authentication material can be captured and reused. Detection therefore concentrates on the network and the file internals rather than on the payload, looking for office applications making outbound requests to internet hosts that are not part of the organisation's template infrastructure, for template references in the relationship parts of recently received documents, and for documents whose only meaningful content is an external pointer.

beginner.definition: Office documents can point at a template stored somewhere else, which is a blueprint the program fetches when the file opens. Attackers change that pointer so the file quietly downloads harmful content, or so it makes your computer prove its identity to a server they control.
beginner.whyItMatters: The harmful code is not inside the file, so a scan of the document finds nothing wrong. The download happens only when the file is opened, usually from an email attachment. Reviewers who check for macros will see a clean document and may approve it. There is also a version of the attack that steals login information rather than running code, and it does not need the user to enable anything. If you only look at the file, you miss the part that matters.
howItWorks: The attacker takes a normal document and edits the part that records where its template lives.
They change that reference to point at a web address on a server they control.
The file is sent to the victim, often as an attachment in a message that looks routine.
When the victim opens it, the office program follows the reference and downloads the template.
The downloaded content carries the harmful code, which then runs on the victim's computer.
In the rich text variant, the template instruction is edited so a simple text search does not match it.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat where each resident is allowed to borrow a spare key from a box in the hallway. A new note appears on the fridge saying the spare key has moved to a locker in another building. The note looks official and the handwriting is neat, so a resident walks over and asks at that building for the key. Nobody broke in. The flat's own rule about spare keys carried the person to a place the residents never controlled.
takeaways: A clean-looking document can still cause a download when it is opened.
Watch network traffic from office programs to internet hosts you do not recognise.
Treat unexpected template references inside received documents as suspicious.

objectives: Explain how an office document stores a reference to an external template resource.
Describe why template injection evades static scanning of the document itself.
Explain how a remote template reference can be used to capture authentication material.
Identify the document parts and relationship entries that reveal a modified template reference.
Describe the network telemetry that shows an office application fetching remote content.
